records.origins: The family claims descent from Gilbert le Grosveneur, who came over with William the Conqueror, and has been seated at Eaton, Cheshire, since the 1440s. In 1677 Sir Thomas Grosvenor, 3rd Baronet, married the twelve-year-old heiress Mary Davies, whose manor of Ebury became Mayfair, Belgravia and Pimlico.
records.role_summary: No documented direct involvement in slavery by the main ducal line. The cross-check found one link in a junior branch: Richard Grosvenor (1762–1819), son of the 1st Earl Grosvenor's younger brother Thomas, married the Drax heiress, took the name Erle-Drax-Grosvenor and owned Drax Hall in Barbados. As an MP he strongly opposed the 1807 bill to abolish the slave trade (per LBS).

roleDetail.d: Per UCL LBS, Richard Erle-Drax-Grosvenor is listed as owner of Drax Hall (St George) and Staple Grove (Christ Church), Barbados, until 1819; his son and then his son-in-law John Sawbridge Erle-Drax inherited.
LBS (citing the History of Parliament) records that he strongly opposed the 1807 bill to abolish the slave trade.

Searches of LBS by surname and keyword (Grosvenor, Westminster, Eaton Hall) returned no compensation claim, mortgage or trusteeship for the Earls Grosvenor or Dukes of Westminster. Grosvenor Square appears in LBS only as the London address of many West India proprietors.

records.legacy: The Grosvenor Estate (c. 300 acres of Mayfair and Belgravia) is run by Grosvenor Group for the 7th Duke and family trusts, alongside the Eaton estate in Cheshire and Liverpool ONE. The Drax Hall branch passed out of the Grosvenor name in 1828; the plantation is still owned by the Drax family today.

records.name: Cadogan family (Earls Cadogan)
records.scaleNote: The Chelsea estate came from Sir Hans Sloane, whose income included his wife's Jamaican sugar plantations; the 1st Earl Cadogan lent £20,500 in 1774 on a Grenada estate and its enslaved people (per LBS).
records.origins: Sir Hans Sloane — physician in Jamaica in 1687–89 and later President of the Royal Society — bought the manor of Chelsea in 1712. In 1717 his daughter Elizabeth married Charles Cadogan, later 2nd Baron Cadogan, and the Sloane estate in Chelsea passed to the Cadogans, who still own it.
records.role_summary: Sloane married the widow of a Jamaican planter in 1695 and drew income from her sugar plantations worked by enslaved people until her death in 1724; historians link that money to his collection and to the purchase of Chelsea. His grandson Charles Sloane Cadogan, later 1st Earl Cadogan, appears in UCL LBS as a mortgagee: in 1774 he lent £20,500 to buy a 320-acre estate in St George's, Grenada, 'with the enslaved people on it'.

roleDetail.d: Sloane's wife Elizabeth Langley Rose was heiress to Jamaican sugar plantations; the London Society and Wikipedia say their income helped fund his collecting and the purchase of Chelsea.
Per LBS, on 31 March 1774 Charles Sloane Cadogan lent £20,500 to Sir Robert Cockburn, Sir George Colebrooke, John Stewart and John Nelson to buy a 320-acre Grenada estate and its enslaved people.
No Cadogan earl appears as an awardee in the 1830s compensation records (LBS search by surname).

records.legacy: Cadogan owns c. 93 acres of Chelsea and Knightsbridge — Sloane Square, Sloane Street, Cadogan Square, Hans Town — run by Cadogan Group for the 9th Earl and family trusts. Sloane's collection founded the British Museum, which in 2020 moved his bust and relabelled it to note his links to slavery.

legacyDetail.d: Sloane Square, Hans Place and Hans Crescent commemorate Sloane; Cadogan Square and Cadogan Hall commemorate the earls.

records.name: Howard de Walden family (Marylebone estate; Ellis & Portland lines)
records.scaleNote: Per LBS, Charles Rose Ellis, Lord Seaford — father of the 6th Baron Howard de Walden — was awarded c. £18,100 for five Jamaican estates; Henry Bentinck, 1st Duke of Portland, ancestor of the Portland line that held Marylebone, died Governor of Jamaica owning 287 enslaved people (1726).
records.origins: The Marylebone estate was bought by John Holles, Duke of Newcastle, in 1708 and passed through his daughter Henrietta Cavendish Holles, who married Edward Harley, and then their daughter Margaret to the Dukes of Portland (the 'Portland Estate'). When the 5th Duke of Portland died in 1879 it went to his sister Lucy, widow of the 6th Baron Howard de Walden, and so to the Ellis (later Scott-Ellis) line.
records.role_summary: Both lines that met in the estate were tied to Caribbean slavery. On the Ellis side, Charles Rose Ellis, Lord Seaford, was a leader of the West India interest in Parliament; LBS records five Jamaican compensation awards to him, and his son the 6th Baron Howard de Walden kept the Jamaican estates as an absentee owner into the 1860s. On the Portland side, Henry Bentinck, 1st Duke of Portland, lost heavily in the South Sea Bubble and died in 1726 as Governor of Jamaica owning 287 enslaved people. Robert Harley, the father-in-law of the estate heiress, founded the South Sea Company in 1711.

roleDetail.d: Per LBS, Lord Seaford was awarded money as owner for Shettlewood Pen, Crawle Pen, Ellis Caymanas, and New and Old Montpelier in Jamaica — c. £18,100 in total.

LBS says Charles Augustus Ellis, 6th Baron Howard de Walden, inherited his father's Jamaican property after emancipation, stayed an absentee owner into the 1860s, and was also left an interest in Fort George estate by a cousin.

Per LBS, the 1st Duke of Portland borrowed against South Sea stock, became Governor of Jamaica in 1721 and died there in 1726; his Jamaican probate listed 287 enslaved people valued at £8,774 Jamaican currency.

roleDetail.t: Harley and the South Sea Company.
roleDetail.d: The National Trust's 2020 report (Wimpole entry) notes that Robert Harley, 1st Earl of Oxford, set up the South Sea Company in 1711; his son married the Marylebone heiress, and Harley Street is named for the family.

records.legacy: The Howard de Walden Estate owns c. 92 acres of Marylebone — Harley Street, Wimpole Street, Cavendish Square, Portland Place — and is owned by the descendants of the 9th Baron's four daughters. The street names record the Holles, Harley, Cavendish and Bentinck (Portland) owners.

legacyDetail.d: The estate built up Harley Street as London's private medical district in the 20th century.

records.name: Montagu Douglas Scott family (Dukes of Buccleuch; Montagu inheritance)
records.scaleNote: The Montagu estates (Boughton) came to Buccleuch through the 3rd Duke's 1767 marriage to Lady Elizabeth Montagu, granddaughter of the 2nd Duke of Montagu, who received a 1722 royal grant of St Lucia and St Vincent and lost c. £40,000 on a failed colonising expedition; no LBS claim was found for any Duke of Buccleuch.
records.base: Boughton House, Northamptonshire (also Bowhill & Drumlanrig, Scotland)
records.origins: Anne Scott, Countess of Buccleuch, married James, Duke of Monmouth, eldest illegitimate son of Charles II, in 1663; the dukedom of Buccleuch survived Monmouth's execution in 1685. In 1767 Henry Scott, 3rd Duke, married Elizabeth Montagu, granddaughter and heir of John, 2nd Duke of Montagu, bringing Boughton House and the Montagu estates, and in 1810 he inherited the Queensberry dukedom and Drumlanrig.
records.role_summary: The cross-check found no slave-ownership or compensation for the Dukes of Buccleuch. The Montagu inheritance carries one colonial project: in 1722 George I granted the islands of St Lucia and St Vincent to John, 2nd Duke of Montagu, who sent Nathaniel Uring with seven ships of settlers. French troops from Martinique forced them out within weeks, and Montagu reportedly lost c. £40,000. The same duke paid for the education of Ignatius Sancho and supported the Jamaican scholar Francis Williams.

roleDetail.d: Letters patent of 22 June 1722 made Montagu proprietor and governor of St Lucia and St Vincent; the settlement at Petit Carenage was abandoned under French pressure (Wikipedia; DNB).
Britain's other Windward settlements of the period became slave plantations; whether Montagu's colony would have relied on enslaved labour is not shown in the sources found.
Montagu financed the education of Ignatius Sancho, later a butler in the Montagu household, and supported Francis Williams.

records.legacy: The 10th Duke chairs the Buccleuch Group and owns c. 200,000 acres in Scotland plus Boughton in Northamptonshire, making him one of Britain's largest private landowners. Shrubsole's 2019 coverage names the Boughton estate among England's great aristocratic holdings.

legacyDetail.d: The 5th Duke held 460,108 acres in England and Scotland, per Bateman's 'Great Landowners'.

records.name: Cavendish family (Dukes of Devonshire)
records.scaleNote: The National Trust's 2020 report (Hardwick Hall) lists colonial investments (Somers Island, Russia, North-West Passage and East India companies) and a female-line kin tie to the Lascelles; the only LBS entry is an unsuccessful Trinidad claim by a grandson of the 4th Duke.
records.origins: Sir William Cavendish, a commissioner in Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries, married Bess of Hardwick and bought Chatsworth in 1549. Their son William became 1st Earl of Devonshire (1618); the 4th Earl was made Duke of Devonshire in 1694 for backing William III. Later marriages brought Bolton Abbey, Lismore in Ireland, and Eastbourne.
records.role_summary: The National Trust's 2020 report finds colonial but not slave-owning ties: the 1st Earl of Devonshire invested in the Somers Island (Bermuda) Company, the Russia and North-West Passage companies and the East India Company. A grandson of the 4th Duke, Lord William Cavendish-Bentinck, made an unsuccessful Trinidad compensation claim as an incumbrancer, and a granddaughter of the 5th Duke married into the slave-owning Lascelles family. No compensation award to a Duke of Devonshire was found.

roleDetail.d: The 1st Earl invested in the Somers Island Company (NT 2020); Devonshire Parish, Bermuda, is named after him. Enslaved Africans were held in Bermuda from the 1610s.
Lord William Cavendish-Bentinck, grandson of the 4th Duke and later Governor-General of India, claimed unsuccessfully as incumbrancer on L'Amitié, Trinidad (LBS claim Trinidad 1684).

records.name: Brydges family (Dukes of Chandos)
records.scaleNote: The 1st Duke sat on the Royal African Company board (1720–25), years in which it shipped over 12,000 enslaved Africans, three voyages on the ship 'Chandos' carrying 1,473 people; the 3rd Duke was joint owner of Hope Estate, Jamaica (1777–89), whose 1836 compensation (£6,630) went to his grandson (LBS; NT 2020).
records.origins: The Brydges were Barons Chandos from 1554. James Brydges made an enormous fortune — reportedly c. £600,000 — as Paymaster of the Forces (1705–13) during Marlborough's wars, built Cannons at Edgware and was created Duke of Chandos in 1719.
records.role_summary: In the 1720 investor wave the 1st Duke took a large stake in the Royal African Company and joined its board (1720–25). In those five years the company transported over 12,000 enslaved Africans, including 1,473 on three voyages of the ship 'Chandos', named for him. He also speculated heavily in South Sea stock. His son's son James, 3rd Duke, married Anna Eliza Elletson, widow of a Jamaican enslaver, and became joint owner of Hope Estate. Through their daughter, Hope passed to the Dukes of Buckingham and Chandos; the 2nd Duke of Buckingham received its 1836 compensation and chaired the West India Committee.

roleDetail.d: St Andrews' Legacies of Empire project: Chandos's 'large personal stake gave him a seat on the board', 1720–25; the 'Chandos' made three voyages with 1,473 people, about 10% of whom died.
Per the History of Parliament, he realised £30,000 selling stock in March 1720, held c. £300,000 by May and lost heavily in the crash.

LBS: the 3rd Duke was joint owner of Hope Estate (St Andrew) 1777–89; in 1836 compensation of £6,630 5s 6d for its enslaved people went to his grandson Richard, later 2nd Duke of Buckingham and Chandos (NT 2020, Stowe).

records.legacy: The money did not last. Cannons was sold and demolished in 1747; the dukedom became extinct in 1789; the Grenville heirs went bankrupt and sold the contents of Stowe in 1848, and the Buckingham dukedom ended in 1889. Stowe is now a school with National Trust gardens. Chandos's £1,000 endowment of St Andrews' Chandos Chair (1720), now in abeyance, is under review by the university's legacies project.

legacyDetail.d: Into Cannons (demolished), South Sea losses, the Cavendish Square scheme and, through the Hope Estate inheritance, to the Grenvilles of Stowe, whose debts ended in the 1848 'great Stowe sale'.
The Chandos Chair of Medicine and Anatomy at St Andrews (1722) has been in abeyance since January 2020.

records.name: The Crown, the Crown Estate & the Duchies of Cornwall and Lancaster (House of Windsor)
records.scaleNote: Charles II chartered the Company of Royal Adventurers (1660/1663) and the Royal African Company (1672) with his brother James as governor; William III received £1,000 of RAC stock (1689); the Crown's landholdings descend from these monarchs.
records.lifespan: 1066–present (Duchy of Cornwall 1337; Duchy of Lancaster 1399; Crown Estate 1760)
records.origins: The monarch's lands are held in three ways today. The Crown Estate holds hereditary Crown lands surrendered to the Treasury by George III in 1760 in return for the Civil List. The Duchy of Lancaster (1399) is the sovereign's private income, and the Duchy of Cornwall (1337) is the heir's. The Stuart restoration of 1660 put the Crown at the centre of the English slave trade.
records.role_summary: Charles II granted the charters of the Company of Royal Adventurers into Africa and, in 1672, the Royal African Company, with his brother James, Duke of York, as governor and largest shareholder. Royal family members were founding subscribers. In 1689 Edward Colston transferred £1,000 of RAC stock to William III, and Queen Anne's government took a share in the 1713 asiento. King Charles III backed independent research into the monarchy's links to slavery in 2023.

roleDetail.d: The 1672 RAC charter names James, Duke of York, and Prince Rupert among officers and subscribers.
The 1689 Colston-to-William III RAC share transfer was found by historian Brooke Newman and published by the Guardian in 2023.

A University of Manchester / Historic Royal Palaces PhD (Camilla de Koning, from 2022) has full access to the Royal Archives; completion was expected in 2026, and findings had not been published as of late 2026.

records.legacy: The Crown Estate (portfolio c. £15bn) pays its profits to the Treasury, part of which returns as the Sovereign Grant; the Duchy of Lancaster provides the King's private income and the Duchy of Cornwall the Prince of Wales's. Shrubsole estimates the Crown holds c. 1.4% of England.

legacyDetail.d: Charles III expressed 'personal sorrow' at slavery (Kigali, 2022); in Jamaica in 2022 Prince William expressed 'profound sorrow', without a formal apology.
Caribbean reparations campaigners, including CARICOM's Reparations Commission, have pressed the British state and monarchy for a formal apology.

records.name: Who Owns England? (Guy Shrubsole, 2019)
records.description: Campaigner Guy Shrubsole's book and website (whoownsengland.org), based on Land Registry data, FOI requests and estate maps, estimated in 2019 that about half of England is owned by under 1% of the population — c. 25,000 landowners, mainly aristocrats and corporations. By his estimate, aristocracy and gentry own c. 30% of England; corporations c. 18%; 'new money' oligarchs, City financiers and industrialists c. 17%; the public sector c. 8.5%; homeowners c. 5%; conservation charities c. 2%; the Crown c. 1.4%; and the Church of England c. 0.5%. Roughly 17% is unregistered and so unaccounted for. This round's cross-check found documented slavery links for a minority of the largest old landed families (Cadogan, Howard de Walden, the Chandos heirs, the Crown) and indirect or no links for most others.
